title: Social Media and Fake News in the 2016 Election
screen_reason: Reports several quantitative shares with denominators: the share of survey respondents who recalled seeing fake news headlines (15%), the share of a random sample of articles from 65 fake news sites categorised as false (just under 55%), and per-adult exposure benchmarks from web browsing data (0.64 impressions per adult) and from survey recall (1.14 articles per adult). Descriptive prevalence/exposure, not a detection or intervention study.

estimates.platform: Post-election online survey (SurveyMonkey Audience Panel); headlines circulated on social media
estimates.date: week of November 28, 2016 (survey); headlines from the three months before the 8 November 2016 election
estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who recalled seeing fake news headlines that actually circulated before the 2016 election
estimates.value_raw: 15 percent of survey respondents recalled seeing the Fake stories
estimates.denominator: 1,208 US adults aged 18+ surveyed online (SurveyMonkey Audience Panel), weighted for national representativeness; each respondent saw 3 randomly assigned headlines from the Fake category and the share is averaged across headlines
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to “Do you recall seeing this reported or discussed prior to the election?” for a headline drawn from the “Fake” categories (six fake stories named in mainstream media coverage of fake news, plus the four most recent pre-election headlines from each of Snopes and PolitiFact deemed unambiguously false)
estimates.misinfo_def: “We define ‘fake news’ to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.”
estimates.source_quote: After weighting for national representativeness, 15 percent of survey respondents recalled seeing the Fake stories, and 8 percent both recalled seeing the story and said they believed it.
estimates.page_loc: p. 227, section “Exposure to Fake News”; Figure 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported recall by the respondent (hence self_report). The headlines shown were selected against a fact-checker standard: Snopes and PolitiFact ratings (“deemed to be unambiguously false”) plus fake news stories named in New York Times, Wall Street Journal and BuzzFeed coverage. No inter-coder reliability is reported.
estimates.moderator_quote: During the week of November 28, 2016, we conducted an online survey of 1208 US adults aged 18 and over using the SurveyMonkey platform. The sample was drawn from SurveyMonkey’s Audience Panel, an opt-in panel
estimates.notes: The paper's headline self-reported exposure figure. The authors stress it is inflated by false recall: the placebo (never-circulated) headlines were recalled at 14%, so the placebo-differenced true recall rate is only about 1.2 percentage points per headline. Recorded as a separate row below.

estimates.measure_type: % of US adults who recalled seeing invented placebo fake news headlines that never circulated (false-recall benchmark)
estimates.value_raw: about 14 percent of people report seeing the placebo stories, and about 8 percent report seeing and believing them
estimates.denominator: 1,208 US adults aged 18+ surveyed online (SurveyMonkey Audience Panel), weighted for national representativeness; each respondent saw 3 randomly assigned Placebo headlines
estimates.definition: Respondent answered yes to “Do you recall seeing this reported or discussed prior to the election?” for one of three invented damaging fake headlines that the authors confirmed had never circulated
estimates.misinfo_def: “We define ‘fake news’ to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.”
estimates.source_quote: By comparison, about 14 percent of people report seeing the placebo stories, and about 8 percent report seeing and believing them.
estimates.page_loc: p. 227, section “Exposure to Fake News”; Figure 5
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Self-reported recall by the respondent (hence self_report). The placebo headlines were invented by the authors and verified via Google searches never to have appeared in actual fake news articles; they were chosen in a pilot to be about as believable as the “Small Fake” stories.
estimates.moderator_quote: The fifth and final category contains invented “Placebo” fake news headlines... We invented three damaging fake headlines that could apply to either Clinton or Trump, then randomized whether a survey respondent saw the pro-Clinton or pro-Trump version.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: this is not an exposure estimate; it is the study's false-recall control. It is recorded so the 15% row is not read at face value, and it should be excluded from any prevalence pool. Flagged borderline=true and definition_variant=true for that reason.

estimates.date: month around the 2016 US presidential election (late October to late November 2016)
estimates.measure_type: % of a random sample of articles from 65 fake news websites that were categorised as false
estimates.denominator: a random sample of articles drawn from the 65 major fake news sites listed by Zimdars (2016) and Brayton (2016); sample size not reported
estimates.definition: Article coded false “either because the claim was refuted by a mainstream news site or fact-checking organization, or because the claim was not covered on any other sites despite being important enough that it would have been covered on other sites if it were true”
estimates.misinfo_def: “We define ‘fake news’ to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.”
estimates.n: random sample of articles from 65 fake news sites (N not reported)
estimates.source_quote: Furthermore, not all content on these 65 sites is false: in a random sample of articles from these sites, we categorized just under 55 percent as false, either because the claim was refuted by a mainstream news site or fact-checking organization, or because the claim was not covered on any other sites despite being important enough that it would have been covered on other sites if it were true.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Authors coded each sampled article against mainstream news coverage and fact-checking organisations; no coder count, procedure detail or reliability statistic reported
estimates.moderator_quote: The lower part of the graph presents web traffic sources for a list of 65 major fake news sites, which we gathered from lists compiled by Zimdars (2016) and Brayton (2016).
estimates.notes: R3 applies: the denominator is articles on sites already designated as fake news sites, so this is falsity WITHIN a misinformation-only sample, not a population prevalence (within_misinfo_content=true). Value is qualified (“just under 55 percent”); the abstract-style summary on p. 212 words it as “just over half of articles appear to be false”. No denominator N is reported for the random sample, and no reliability statistics.

estimates.platform: 65 fake news websites (Alexa web browsing data)
estimates.date: month around the 2016 US presidential election (late October to late November 2016)
estimates.measure_type: impressions on 65 fake news websites per US adult in the month around the election
estimates.value_raw: 159 million impressions on the 65 websites ... or 0.64 impressions per adult
estimates.denominator: 248 million American adults (the paper reports exposure “as average exposure for each of the 248 million American adults”)
estimates.definition: An impression on any of the 65 major fake news sites compiled from the Zimdars (2016) and Brayton (2016) lists, measured by Alexa web traffic data (browser extensions plus site measurement services; excludes mobile browsing and content viewed inside social media feeds)
estimates.misinfo_def: “We define ‘fake news’ to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.”
estimates.source_quote: For the month around the 2016 election, there were 159 million impressions on the 65 websites in the bottom part of Figure 3, or 0.64 impressions per adult. This is dwarfed by the 3 billion impressions on the 665 top news websites over the same period.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: A list of 65 major fake news sites gathered from lists compiled by Zimdars (2016) and Brayton (2016); the authors note there is no definitive list and one might disagree about particular sites
estimates.moderator_quote: Figure 3 presents web traffic sources for the month around the 2016 US presidential election (late October through late November) from Alexa (alexa.com), which gathers data from browser extensions installed on people’s computers as well as from measurement services offered to websites. These data exclude mobile browsing and do not capture news viewed directly on social media sites
estimates.notes: Source-level (domain list) measure, so breadth is blank. Only about 55% of the content on these sites was judged false (see the CONTENT row), so this over-counts false-article exposure. The comparison figure of 3 billion impressions on the 665 top news sites is given, but a diet-share (159m / 3.16bn) would be a computed ratio and is not extracted per R8.

estimates.platform: Fake news articles circulating on Facebook, measured via post-election survey recall
estimates.date: three months before the 8 November 2016 election (article database); survey week of November 28, 2016
estimates.measure_type: average number of fake news articles from the study database that the average US adult saw and remembered
estimates.value_raw: the average adult saw and remembered 0.03/million × 38 million ≈ 1.14 fake news articles from our fake news database
estimates.denominator: 248 million American adults; projection from the placebo-differenced recall rate (1.2 percentage points per average Fake headline, average 0.386 million Facebook shares) applied to the 38 million Facebook shares of the 156 articles in the fake news database
estimates.definition: An article from the authors' 156-article fake news database (Snopes, PolitiFact and BuzzFeed lists) that a respondent both saw and recalled seeing, net of the placebo false-recall rate
estimates.misinfo_def: “We define ‘fake news’ to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.”
estimates.source_quote: Given that the Fake articles in our database had 38 million Facebook shares, this implies that the average adult saw and remembered 0.03/million × 38 million ≈ 1.14 fake news articles from our fake news database.
estimates.ground_truth_detail: 156-article database scraped from the Donald Trump and Hillary Clinton tags on Snopes, the 2016 presidential election tag on PolitiFact, and BuzzFeed's list of 21 high-engagement fake news articles; the authors state the list is “reasonable but probably not comprehensive”
estimates.moderator_quote: We provide three benchmarks for election-period fake news exposure, which we report as average exposure for each of the 248 million American adults.
estimates.notes: ADJUDICATOR: this is the paper's headline exposure number and is stated verbatim, but it is a linear extrapolation, not a measurement: it multiplies a placebo-differenced per-headline recall rate (1.2 pp, 95% CI excluding differences above 2.9 pp) by total Facebook shares of the database. It is bounded below by database incompleteness and above by shares-to-reads assumptions. Confidence low, borderline true.

missed_or_uncertain: NOT extracted, with reasons. (1) “the 38 million shares of fake news in our database translate into 760 million page visits, or about three visits per US adult” (p. 226): the authors explicitly build this on an assumed upper bound of 20 page visits per Facebook share taken from unrelated non-academic sources (Eventbrite, a blog post, a Renren study), so it is an assumption-driven upper bound rather than an estimate of what was observed. (2) “8 percent both recalled seeing the story and said they believed it”: a recall-and-belief conjunction; the protocol excludes belief measures, and this is not a clean exposure share. (3) Figure 3 traffic-source shares (social media 41.8% of traffic to fake news sites vs 10.1% for top news sites; search 22.0%/30.6%; direct 30.5%/48.7%): these are shares of traffic BY REFERRAL SOURCE, not shares of content or consumption that is false, so they do not measure misinformation prevalence. (4) The 156-article database with 30.3 million pro-Trump and 7.6 million pro-Clinton Facebook shares: an all-false corpus with no denominator, excluded by protocol. (5) “62 percent of US adults get news on social media”, the Pew trust figures, the Gallup trust series and the Bakshy et al. ideological-segregation shares: all cited from other publications, excluded per R8. (6) “only 14 percent of American adults viewed social media as their ‘most important’ source of election news” (Figure 4): a news-source share, not a misinformation measure. (7) Figure 5 is read only through the values stated in the text (Fake 15%/8%, Placebo 14%/8%); the Big True and Small True bar values are not given numerically in the text and were not eyeballed off the figure. (8) Tables 1 and 2 report belief and discernment regressions only, which the protocol excludes. (9) The 1.2 percentage-point Fake-minus-Placebo difference is a difference, not a share, so no row.

rob.design: Three data sources. (a) Opt-in online survey of 1,208 US adults 18+ from the SurveyMonkey Audience Panel, fielded the week of 28 November 2016; each respondent saw 15 of 30 headlines randomly drawn from five categories (Big Fake, Small Fake, Big True, Small True, Placebo); responses reweighted to the national adult population on ten characteristics including income, education, gender, age, ethnicity, party and news-consumption frequency; no response rate reported, and the authors note opt-in panels typically do not give nationally representative results even after reweighting, with their unweighted sample disproportionately well-educated, female, Caucasian and web/social-media-heavy. (b) A database of 156 fake news articles scraped from Snopes (138 articles), PolitiFact and a BuzzFeed list of 21, with Facebook share counts from BuzzSumo as of early December 2016; the authors report imperfect overlap between the three lists and state the database is probably not comprehensive. (c) Alexa web traffic for the top 690 US news sites and 65 fake news sites from lists by Zimdars (2016) and Brayton (2016), for the month around the election, excluding mobile browsing and in-feed views. Article falsity coding on the 65 sites was done by the authors against mainstream coverage and fact-checkers; no coder count, coding protocol detail or inter-coder reliability statistic is reported anywhere in the paper.
rob.item6_quote: We define “fake news” to be news articles that are intentionally and verifiably false, and could mislead readers.
rob.item10_quote: After weighting for national representativeness, 15 percent of survey respondents recalled seeing the Fake stories, and 8 percent both recalled seeing the story and said they believed it.
